VBO:0200810.summary: Self-confident and even-tempered, Landseers often form strong attachments to their people while keeping watch over home. Their affinity for water has also taken them into rescue work, while the European Continental breed’s guard-and-companion role traces to Germany and Switzerland.
VBO:0200810.historicalRoots: European Continental Landseer developed in Germany and Switzerland from the old white-and-black Newfoundland lineage.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 226: Landseer (European Continental Type)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 226 identifies the European Continental Landseer with Germany/Switzerland origin and guard-dog and companion utilization.

sources.title: VDH Landseer breed profile
sources.evidence: VDH describes Landseers as self-confident, even-tempered and watchful, strongly attached to people, fond of water and active in water rescue.

VBO:0200810.shortDescription: Self-confident and even-tempered, this watchful companion has strong ties to people and a notable love of water.

VBO:0200380.summary: Attentive, self-confident and friendly, the Continental Bulldog developed in Switzerland as an active companion. English Bulldog and Old English Bulldog crosses shaped a breed that kept recognizable bulldog character while placing more emphasis on athletic movement.
VBO:0200380.historicalRoots: Swiss breed developed from English Bulldog and Old English Bulldog crosses as a medium-sized, active bull-type dog.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 369: Continental Bulldog
sources.evidence: FCI No. 369 gives Swiss origin; English Bulldog and Old English Bulldog crosses in development; companion/family utilization; attentive, self-confident, friendly temperament; active, athletic movement. Its conformation goal is not an individual breathing guarantee.

VBO:0200380.shortDescription: Attentive, self-confident and friendly, this Swiss bulldog was developed as an active companion.

VBO:0200703.summary: Spirited and affectionate, the Irish Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier has the resourcefulness of an old farm dog. For generations it helped small Irish farmers with vermin and rough-country work, long before the breed gained formal recognition.
VBO:0200703.historicalRoots: Irish farm terrier with textual evidence of soft-coated dogs for at least two centuries; Irish Kennel Club recognition in 1937.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 40: Irish Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier
sources.evidence: Irish origin; small farmers used the breed to kill vermin and help farm work, and historically hunted badgers and otters. Spirited, game, good-tempered, affectionate, loyal and intelligent. Soft silky wheaten single coat, small folded ears, naturally full tail not carried over back.

VBO:0200703.shortDescription: Spirited and affectionate, this Irish farm terrier once helped control vermin and hunt in rough country.

VBO:0200340.summary: Quick, alert and lively, the smooth-haired Chihuahua can be remarkably bold for a tiny companion. The breed takes its name from Mexico’s largest state; this close-coated variety shares the same spirited character as the recognized long-haired Chihuahua.
VBO:0200340.historicalRoots: Mexican toy companion; ancient lineage claims in the FCI historical section are presented as theories rather than proven facts.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 218: Chihuahua, Smooth-Haired
sources.evidence: FCI No. 218 describes quick, alert, lively and courageous temperament; companion use, Mexico origin and name from Chihuahua state; smooth- and long-haired varieties.

VBO:0200340.shortDescription: Quick, alert and lively, the smooth-haired Chihuahua brings surprising courage to its companion role.

VBO:0201357.summary: Composed and patient, the Tosa is known for quiet boldness. Bred in Japan’s Tosa region from Shikoku-ken and several Western breeds, it emerged from a historical fighting tradition; the FCI now recognizes its watchdog role.
VBO:0201357.historicalRoots: Japanese molossoid developed in the Tosa region; historically used in dog fighting, now listed by FCI as watchdog.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 260: Tosa
sources.evidence: FCI No. 260 describes patience, composure, boldness and courage; Tosa-region origin, Shikoku-ken and sequential Western breed crosses, former fighting use and current watchdog utilization.

VBO:0201357.shortDescription: Patient and composed yet bold, the Tosa is a Japanese mastiff whose role shifted from fighting to watching.

VBO:0200712.summary: Watchful and responsive, the Cane Corso has long worked close to people in southern Italy, especially Apulia. Its roles included guarding property and livestock, moving cattle and accompanying big-game hunters; that varied work called for agility as well as strength.
VBO:0200712.historicalRoots: Italian molossoid preserved especially in southern Italy and Apulia, historically a versatile farm and hunting dog.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 343: Italian Cane Corso
sources.evidence: FCI No. 343 documents southern Italian prevalence especially Apulia, guardian of property and livestock, responsiveness and agility, historical cattle herding and big-game hunting.

VBO:0200712.shortDescription: Watchful and responsive, the Cane Corso has guarded southern Italian farms and helped with cattle and hunting.

VBO:0201085.summary: Steady and self-assured, the Presa Canario is attentive to its surroundings and can be reserved with strangers. It developed on Tenerife and Gran Canaria, where historical records describe its work guarding and handling cattle; a deep bark and vigilant stance suit that role.
VBO:0201085.historicalRoots: Canary Islands molossoid developed chiefly on Tenerife and Gran Canaria for cattle protection.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 346: Presa Canario
sources.evidence: FCI No. 346 documents origin on Tenerife and Gran Canaria, traditional cattle guarding and handling, balanced self-assurance, attentiveness, stranger reserve, deep bark and vigilant stance.

VBO:0201085.shortDescription: Self-assured and attentive, the Presa Canario has a long tradition of guarding and handling cattle.

VBO:0200382.summary: Lively and engaging, the Papillon retains the spirit of a little spaniel beneath its delicate look. Continental Toy Spaniels appear in European paintings for centuries; the erect-eared Papillon variety became fashionable later than its drop-eared relative.
VBO:0200382.historicalRoots: French and Belgian Continental Toy Spaniel lineage depicted in European Renaissance art; erect-ear Papillon developed later than drop-ear Phalène.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 77: Continental Toy Spaniel, Papillon - With Erect Ears
sources.evidence: France and Belgium origin. The Papillon variety has high-set erect, fringed butterfly-shaped ears; Phalène is the distinct drop-eared variety. Fine-boned active toy with abundant silky white-predominant coat and plumed high-set tail.

sources.title: Papillon Club of America: A Brief History of the Papillon
sources.evidence: Breed-club historical account traces Continental Toy Spaniels through Western European paintings since the 16th century and explains the later fashion for erect butterfly ears.

sources.title: Papillon Club of America: Dog or Butterfly?
sources.evidence: Breed-club profile describes lively companion character and spaniel-like interest in field scents; distinguishes erect-ear Papillon from drop-ear Phalène.

VBO:0200382.shortDescription: Lively and engaging, the erect-eared Papillon keeps a little spaniel’s alert curiosity and companion spirit.

VBO:0201158.summary: Saarloos Wolfhonden are lively, independent dogs whose devotion to familiar people can sit beside reserve with strangers and a preference to avoid unfamiliar situations. Leendert Saarloos developed the breed from a German Shepherd–wolf cross; although he sought a working dog, the resulting breed became known for its own distinct character.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 311: Saarloos Wolfhond
sources.evidence: FCI No. 311 documents independent lively character, loyalty to familiar people, reserve with strangers, Leendert Saarloos’s breeding history, wolf-grey coat, erect ears and low sabre tail.

VBO:0201158.shortDescription: Devoted to familiar people yet inclined to retreat from unfamiliar situations, this wolfdog has a strong independent streak.

VBO:0200472.summary: East Siberian Laikas tend to be steady with people while remaining vigorous and independent on a hunt. Their keen scent and strong interest in game developed in the taiga and mountain regions of Central and East Siberia, where the breed has long served as an all-round hunting partner.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 305: East Siberian Laika
sources.evidence: FCI No. 305 describes steady temperament, scent and game detection, hunting independence, friendliness to people, taiga origins, V-shaped pricked ears and sickle/curled tail.

VBO:0200472.shortDescription: A steady companion to people, this Siberian laika becomes a vigorous, independent hunter in taiga and mountain country.

VBO:0201416.summary: West Siberian Laikas are steady and alert, self-confident around strangers and intensely interested in hunting. In forest work, they use a keen nose to seek both feathered and furred game. The breed grew from Khanty and Mansi hunting dogs in the Ural and Siberian forests.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 306: West Siberian Laika
sources.evidence: FCI No. 306 describes steady, alert temperament, self-confidence toward strangers, strong scent and game detection, equal interest in feathered and furred game, and Khanty/Mansi roots in Ural and Siberian forests.

VBO:0201416.shortDescription: Steady and alert, this laika uses a keen nose to seek both feathered and furred game in forest work.

VBO:0200383.summary: Lively and companionable, the Phalène shares the Continental Toy Spaniel’s small, alert presence with the Papillon. Its history reaches back to the drop-eared toy spaniels portrayed in European art before the erect-eared variety became familiar. The name means “moth,” referring to the softly hanging ears.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 77: Phalène
sources.evidence: FCI No. 77 states toy use, lively character, Phalène hanging-ear variety, white-dominant coat and plumed tail; Papillon Club of America records historic drop-eared toy spaniels and the moth-name.

sources.title: Papillon Club of America: A Brief History of the Papillon
sources.evidence: Breed club history records the earlier drop-eared variety and later rise of erect ears.

VBO:0200383.shortDescription: Lively and companionable, this toy spaniel shares a long European companion history with its erect-eared relative.

VBO:0200838.summary: Alert and energetic, the Norwegian Lundehund carries an unusual climbing heritage. On Norway’s steep coastal rocks, these dogs once entered narrow puffin burrows; extra functional toes, folding ears and remarkable flexibility helped with that work. The birds are protected today, so the breed’s old job belongs to its history.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 265: Lundehund
sources.evidence: FCI No. 265 documents alert energetic temperament, puffin-burrow history, extra functional toes, folding ears, red/fawn-white coat and variable ring or hanging tail.

VBO:0200838.shortDescription: An agile coastal climber, the Lundehund once entered narrow puffin burrows using extra toes and unusual flexibility.

VBO:0200235.summary: Briquet Griffon Vendéens are determined, initiative-taking hounds that use a fine nose and a pleasant voice while working through bramble. Traditionally hunting in small packs, they can follow a cold trail, find game and drive it across rough ground. The breed was revived in Vendée after wartime losses.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 19: Briquet Griffon Vendeen
sources.evidence: FCI No. 19 documents a determined, initiative-taking hunter with fine nose, pleasant voice, rough-terrain and bramble agility; cold-track, finding and driving abilities; small-pack use for large game, fox and hare; Grand Griffon Vendéen derivation, 1946 Vendée revival, fawn-white harsh coat, narrow pointed drop ears and a short sabre rather than sickle tail.

VBO:0200235.shortDescription: A determined Vendée hound, the Briquet follows cold trails and drives game through bramble with a fine nose and voice.

VBO:0200775.summary: Kleiner Münsterländers often work with alert friendliness and close attention to their people. In the field they bring persistence and a strong interest in game, with a tradition of searching, pointing and retrieving across woodland, open ground and water. Their development in northern Germany’s Münsterland is documented from the late nineteenth century.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 102: Kleiner Münsterländer
sources.evidence: FCI No. 102 describes intelligent steady friendliness, close cooperation with handler, pointing and retrieving history, high-set hanging ears, brown-white coat and level flagged tail.

VBO:0200775.shortDescription: Friendly and attentive in company, this Münsterland hunter searches, points and retrieves across land and water.

VBO:0200464.summary: Watchful and independent, Dutch Shepherds also have a strong tradition of working closely with people. Their first work included keeping sheep away from crops by patrolling field and road edges, then moving flocks to common grazing. The long-haired variety shares that character and history with the other coat varieties.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 223: Dutch Shepherd Dog, Long-Haired
sources.evidence: FCI No. 223 describes loyal alert independent temperament, historic sheep and crop work, long straight harsh brindle coat, erect ears and hanging tail.

VBO:0200464.shortDescription: A watchful sheepdog once tasked with patrolling field edges to keep flocks out of crops, here in its long-haired coat.

VBO:0200548.summary: French Spaniels are calm and gentle in company but enthusiastic in the field, where their firm point and retrieving ability come to the fore. Their ancestors appear in medieval French hunting accounts; later selection shaped the athletic pointing dog described today.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 175: French Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI No. 175 describes balanced calm gentle temperament, medieval bird-dog lineage, firm pointing and retrieving talent, white-and-brown coat and low undocked tail.

VBO:0200548.shortDescription: Gentle in company and keen in the field, the French Spaniel has a long tradition of pointing and retrieving.

VBO:0200182.summary: Blue Picardy Spaniels tend to be gentle and even-tempered, yet have an athletic side that benefits from regular walks. They worked close enough for hunters to shoot over them and became especially valued for finding woodcock. Recognized separately in 1938, the breed emerged from northern French black-and-white spaniels; its blue-speckled coat remains the clearest distinction from the Picardy Spaniel.
VBO:0200182.historicalRoots: Northern French pointing spaniel, separately standardized in 1938, skilled at woodcock hunting.

sources.title: FCI: Blue Picardy Spaniel (Standard No. 106)
sources.evidence: Gentle even temperament, athletic daily-walk need, work within gun range and particular woodcock skill; line of northern black/white spaniels given separate standard in 1938; silver-gray-black speckled coat, full low tail and eye-level feathered ears.

sources.title: Club des Épagneuls de Picardie et Pont-Audemer: Our Breeds
sources.evidence: Official French breed club describes the Picardy spaniels as close-working hunting dogs across plain, woodland and marsh terrain.

VBO:0200182.shortDescription: Gentle and athletic, this northern French spaniel worked close to hunters and became prized for finding woodcock.

VBO:0201046.summary: Pont-Audemer Spaniels worked close to their hunters, searching and pointing without ranging far ahead. In Normandy’s Vernier marshes they became known for waterfowl work and retrieving, but they also hunted in woods and open country.
VBO:0201046.historicalRoots: Norman pointing and water dog associated with the Vernier marshes and fowl hunting.

sources.title: FCI: Pont-Audemer Spaniel (Standard No. 114)
sources.evidence: French pointing breed; stocky spaniel with characteristic curly topknot and ears, brown-gray mottled coat, low sturdy legs, and medium natural tail carried slightly curved if undocked.

sources.title: Club des Épagneuls de Picardie et Pont-Audemer: Our Breeds
sources.evidence: Official club characterizes its spaniels as close-working dogs rather than distant-ranging hunters.

sources.title: Club des Épagneuls de Picardie et Pont-Audemer: Pont-Audemer Spaniel
sources.evidence: French parent club records waterfowl use in the Vernier marshes, water work with pointing and retrieving, plus woodland and plain hunting.

VBO:0201046.shortDescription: A close-working Norman spaniel, at home searching marshes for waterfowl and retrieving from the water.

VBO:0200465.summary: Rough-haired Dutch Shepherds share the breed’s loyal, alert nature and its habit of working independently while cooperating with a handler. On Dutch farms they patrolled the edges of crops to hold sheep back and kept hens out of kitchen gardens. As flocks declined, Dutch Shepherds also took on police, search and guide work.
VBO:0200465.historicalRoots: Dutch farm shepherd; later police, tracking and guide work as sheep flocks declined.

sources.title: FCI: Dutch Shepherd Dog (Standard No. 223)
sources.evidence: Shared loyal, alert, active, independent working temperament; detailed Dutch farm duties and later police/search/guide uses; short, long and wire-coated varieties; rough coat has harsh beard and brows, visible brindle, erect ears and tail low to hock, never curled.

VBO:0200465.shortDescription: Loyal and alert, this rough-coated Dutch worker once guarded crop edges, tended flocks and worked with its handler.

VBO:0201019.summary: Picardy Spaniels tend to be gentle and even-tempered, with the energy of an athletic pointing dog. Hunters in Picardy valued a keen nose and a steady point for small game across the region’s fields and marshes. The breed remained largely local for generations, then drew renewed interest from hunters who appreciated that versatile field work.
VBO:0201019.historicalRoots: Regional French pointing spaniel used for small game across Picardy's varied terrain.

sources.title: FCI: Picardy Spaniel (Standard No. 108)
sources.evidence: Gentle even temperament, athletic daily-walk need, local Picardy pointing and keen scent for small game, long regional obscurity and renewed hunter interest; brown mottled autumn-leaf coat, eye-level long wavy ears and low tail with two gentle curves.

sources.title: Club des Épagneuls de Picardie et Pont-Audemer: Picardy Spaniel
sources.evidence: French breed club describes Picardy's plains, woods and marshes as the backdrop to this local hunting dog's development.

VBO:0201019.shortDescription: Gentle yet energetic, the Picardy Spaniel used its keen nose and steady point across northern French fields and marshes.

VBO:0200847.summary: Majorca Shepherd Dogs tend to be affectionate and strongly attached to their own person, yet reserved with strangers; that reserve can be especially marked when young. On Mallorca, their working life centered on herding flocks and guarding property.
VBO:0200847.historicalRoots: Mallorcan herding, guarding and farm defense dog; short coat most common of two varieties.

sources.title: FCI: Majorca Shepherd Dog (Standard No. 321, Spanish)
sources.evidence: Spanish standard identifies Mallorcan pastoral/guard use, intelligence, strong loyalty and affection for familiar people, reserve with strangers and marked shyness in youth; black short/long coat varieties, folded drop ears and full undocked tail to hock.

VBO:0200847.shortDescription: Affectionate with its person and reserved with strangers, this Mallorcan shepherd tended flocks and guarded property.

VBO:0200845.summary: Ca de Bou dogs tend to be quiet and self-assured with familiar people, but become sharply watchful when roused. Their history runs from guarding Balearic coastal settlements to bull baiting, which gave the breed its name: “bull dog.”
VBO:0200845.historicalRoots: Mallorcan mastiff used in cattle and property work; historical bull-spectacle use documented.

sources.title: FCI: Ca de Bou (Standard No. 249)
sources.evidence: Quiet, trusting and self-assured at rest but courageous and watchful when roused; historical Balearic guard and bull-fighting accounts; compact medium mastiff body, massive square head, small rose ears, short brindle/fawn/black coat and full low-set tail.

sources.title: Royal Canine Society of Spain: Dogo Mallorquín (Ca de Bou)
sources.evidence: Spanish national registry describes cattle work, guarding farms and historical bull spectacles on Mallorca; complements FCI history without romanticizing fighting.

VBO:0200845.shortDescription: Quiet and self-assured with familiar people, the Ca de Bou becomes keenly watchful when roused.

VBO:0200466.summary: Short-haired Dutch Shepherds share the breed’s watchful, active character and its independent but cooperative working style. On Dutch farms they patrolled field edges to keep sheep from crops and gathered cows for milking. As flocks dwindled, Dutch Shepherds took on police, tracking and guide work; short hair identifies a coat variety.
VBO:0200466.historicalRoots: Dutch farm shepherd later used in search, police and guide roles; short coat variety.

sources.title: FCI: Dutch Shepherd Dog (Standard No. 223)
sources.evidence: Shared loyal, watchful, active and independently cooperative character; Dutch farm boundary, cattle, police/search/guide tasks; short close harsh coat clearly brindled, upright ears and full tail low to hock at rest.

VBO:0200466.shortDescription: Watchful and cooperative, this short-coated Dutch farm worker guided livestock and patrolled crop edges.

VBO:0200285.summary: Castro Laboreiro Dogs are described as loyal and docile with their families, while remaining vigilant over flocks and property. In northern Portugal they guarded livestock against wolves and patrolled as sentinels. Their distinctive alarm bark begins deep and rises into a prolonged higher note, a sound tied to that mountain watch role.
VBO:0200285.historicalRoots: Portuguese mountain livestock guardian from Castro Laboreiro, used against wolf predation.

sources.title: FCI: Castro Laboreiro Dog (Standard No. 170)
sources.evidence: Loyal and docile with family, vigilant patrolling sentinel, flock protection against wolves and distinctive rising alarm bark; northern Portugal origin, wolf/tiger brindle coat, natural low scimitar tail and hanging triangular ears.

VBO:0200285.shortDescription: Loyal to its family and vigilant over flocks, this Portuguese mountain guard dog gives a distinctive rising alarm bark.
